title: ficar and estar
explanation: Both can talk about location or a state, but they are not interchangeable. Use ficar for where something fixed is (a hotel, a city, a street): Onde fica o hotel? Use estar for where a person or a movable thing is right now: Onde está a mala? Estar also names a temporary state (estou bem). Ficar, besides location, can mean to stay or to become: eu fico no hotel (I’m staying), fico feliz (I become / end up happy).

title: ser and estar
explanation: Portuguese has two everyday verbs for English “to be.” ser is for what something is — identity, origin, profession, a lasting quality, the time of day: ela é brasileira, são três horas. estar is for how or where it is right now: ela está no hotel, estou bem. Some adjectives change meaning with the verb (ele é gentil = that’s his nature; ele está gentil = he is being kind at the moment).

title: isto, isso, and aquilo
explanation: These three point at things at different distances. isto is this, near the speaker (in my hands). isso is that, near the listener — and in everyday Brazilian speech it often covers both “this” and “that.” aquilo is that over there, away from both of you. The t in isto is also the sound that sets it apart from isso; see Spelling & sounds.

title: quem and que
explanation: quem asks for a person: Quem é? (Who is it?). que, usually as o que, asks for a thing: O que é isso? (What is that?). They also sound different: que is a plain “kee” [ki]; quem ends in the nasal diphthong [kẽj̃], like tem. See Spelling & sounds.

title: em and de
explanation: A common mix-up is origin versus location. de is of / from: Sou de Nova York (I’m from New York), de onde você é? em is in / at / on: Estou em Nova York, estou no hotel. de also marks possession or what something is made of (a mala do senhor). em almost always contracts with the article: no, na, nos, nas.

title: bom and bem
explanation: bom is an adjective, “good,” and it agrees with the noun: um bom hotel, uma boa tarde, bom dia. bem is an adverb, “well,” and does not change: estou bem, tudo bem, muito bem. English “I’m good” is usually estou bem in Portuguese, not estou bom.

title: tarde and noite
explanation: tarde is the afternoon (from around noon until dusk) and the greeting is boa tarde. noite is night, once it’s dark; the greeting is boa noite, used both as a hello in the evening and as a good-night. tarde is also the word for “late”: é tarde, cheguei tarde. The two greetings are not interchangeable — boa tarde in the afternoon, boa noite at night.

title: o senhor and você
explanation: Both mean “you,” and both take a third-person verb (você é, o senhor é). você is the everyday form in most of Brazil — informal to neutral, used with almost anyone you would first-name in English. o senhor (and a senhora) is the respectful, formal “you”: older people, customers, official or polite situations. The same words, without being used as “you,” can also mean “the gentleman / the lady.”
